articles.title: RF-EMF response modeling of implantable medical electrodes under 1.5T and 3T MRI exposure using a lumped element model approach.
articles.abstract: Accurate assessment of radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) induced heating risks for patients with implantable medical electrodes during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains challenging, particularly when implementing the Tier 4(-) evaluation methodology, outlined in the latest ISO 10974 IS1 Committee Draft for Vote (CDV),, in heterogeneous tissue environments. This work introduces an equivalent lumped element model (LEM) to streamline in vivo RF response modeling of implantable medical electrodes in complicated tissue environments without substantially increasing computational burden. Extensive numerical studies were conducted for generic helical implantable medical electrodes with lead lengths of 400, 500, and 600 mm in homogeneous, heterogeneous, and anatomically realistic tissue environments from the Virtual Population model Ella, at 1.5 T and 3.0 T. The LEM-based approach consistently yielded more accurate estimates of RF-EMF-induced power deposited at the implant hotspot than transfer functions derived from simplified tissue configurations representative of Tier 3 evaluations. In particular, the LEM reproduced the equivalent impedance and transfer function of the detailed implantable medical electrode, enabling efficient evaluation of RF-EMF-induced heating in clinically relevant heterogeneous tissue environment. Experimental validation with a commercial implantable medical electrode further showed close agreement between the LEM-predicted transfer function and measurements of the commercial device. These results indicate that the proposed methodology addresses key limitations of conventional modeling strategies and provides a robust, computationally efficient framework for Tier 4(-) RF-EMF-induced heating risk assessment in clinical MRI exposure.

articles.title: Test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1: a model-based, subject-specific self-supervised motion correction method for robust cardiac T1 mapping.
articles.abstract: Reliable myocardial T1 mapping is essential for quantitative cardiac tissue characterization but remains sensitive to respiratory motion, particularly during free-breathing acquisitions. This study evaluated the test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1, a subject-specific, model-based, self-supervised deep-learning method for motion-robust myocardial T1 mapping.Approach. Seventeen healthy male volunteers aged 20-36 years underwent 3 T cardiac MRI using a 5(3)3 MOLLI acquisition under breath-hold (BH) and free-breathing (FB) conditions. Same-day repeat scans were acquired after a 20 min interval that included removal from and repositioning in the scanner. T1 maps were reconstructed using (1) MBSS-T1, (2) the contrast-agnostic deep-learning registration method SynthMorph, (3) scanner-inline motion correction, and (4) no motion correction. Repeatability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), relative Bland-Altman analysis, within-subject coefficients of variation (CVw), relative 95% repeatability coefficients (RC95), and variance-based bootstrap inference with Holm correction.Main results. All four methods included 17 complete participant-level test-retest pairs under each breathing condition. Under BH conditions, the global ICC point estimates were 0.77, 0.64, 0.65, and 0.60 for MBSS-T1, SynthMorph, scanner-inline correction, and no correction, respectively. Under FB conditions, the corresponding values were 0.41, 0.32, 0.27, and 0.16. MBSS-T1 also had the lowest descriptive CVw under both conditions. However, none of the paired comparisons of absolute test-retest differences was significant after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.623). The smallest Holm-adjusted variance-ratio result was obtained for MBSS-T1 versus no correction under FB conditions (variance ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.68; adjusted p = 0.058), which did not meet the prespecified significance threshold. Significance. MBSS-T1 yielded favourable descriptive repeatability estimates, particularly under FB conditions, but no pairwise comparison remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. These results characterize same-day, same-scanner measurement precision rather than absolute T1 accuracy and require confirmation in larger and more clinically diverse cohorts.

articles.title: The numerical study on cardiac ablation considering dynamic blood flow by high frequency bipolar pulses with determined lethal threshold in vitro.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) is a promising non-thermal energy modality for catheter-based cardiac ablation. Treatment planning using numerical simulations of PFA is important for predicting the ablation region. However, owing to the high voltage-to-electrode distance ratio, thermal effects should be considered during treatment planning. This study aims to analyse the ablation region for cardiac treatment planning considering the thermal effect. APPROACH: this study aimed first to determine the lethal electric field threshold (LEFT) of H9C2 myocardial cells exposed to high-frequency bipolar pulses (HFBPs). Then two simplified pulmonary vein (PV) models with a circular electrode array were constructed to investigate electric field and thermal distributions, accounting for dynamic blood flow and conductivity variation. MAIN RESULTS: cell experimental results showed that under the condition of equivalent energized time, fewer pulses per burst and prolonged interpulse delay of HFBPs can reduce the LEFT of myocardial cells. The LET reached 720 V/cm when applying 120 HFBPs of 1000 μs duration. Numerical simulations revealed that temperature rises sharply when blood flow is neglected, with a maximum temperature of 67 ℃. However, thermal effects are substantially limited (peak temperature of 38.3 ℃) due to blood flow, even when HFBPs with a high voltage-to-electrode distance (1250 V) are applied. The temperature rise rapidly declines and reaches a plateau at higher blood velocities. HFBPs can produce a full circumferential ablation region, and the ablation width increases linearly with rising applied voltage. SIGNIFICANCE: this study demonstrates that dynamic blood flow and conductivity effects should be considered for myocardial ablation assessments, which may assist clinicians in precise pulse selection.

articles.title: External Validation and Clinical Readiness of Imaging Models for Axillary Nodal Metastasis: A Bibliometric Evidence Map with a Nested Full-Text Audit.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the development of imaging research on axillary nodal metastasis and assess external validation claims, clinical readiness reporting, and risk of bias in a nested literature audit. A Web of Science evidence map included 486 imaging-related records published in 2005-2025. A nested audit sampled 76 reports from the original 208 report model article frame. After removal of one non-imaging model, 75 reports were retained. Validation design, reporting features, and selected model risk were examined. Temporal validation was separated in sensitivity analyses; expansion-weighted estimates were conditional on sampling assumptions. Model-related language increased from 2.2% of mapped records in 2005-2011 to 67.6% in 2022-2025. Among 75 audited reports, broad external validation was supported in 36, unclear in two and unsupported in 37; excluding temporal-only validation left 29 supported reports. Reporting codes with targeted corrections identified calibration in 39 reports, decision-curve analysis in 40, reader comparison in ten and prospective evaluation in six. Source review distinguished reporting from model-specific adequacy. All 38 selected-model evaluations were assessed as high risk of bias. Seven of 43 primary evaluation components met 50 participants per outcome class. Imaging-model research has expanded, but independent evaluation and clinical readiness evidence remain uneven in the audited literature. Validation terminology, model-specific reporting, and evaluation design require joint appraisal before clinical translation.

articles.title: Image-Level Splitting Inflates Apparent Performance Through Repeated Patient-Level Variables in Breast Ultrasound AI: A Patient-Grouped Study of Intraductal Papilloma.
articles.abstract: To quantify how image-level rather than patient-level fold assignment inflates the apparent performance of breast ultrasound models, using a clinical task without demonstrable discrimination as a negative control. This retrospective single-centre study included 250 women with intraductal papilloma (IDP; 553 B-mode images; 184 colour Doppler images in 144 patients), 47 (18.8%) with associated atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Radiomics, clinical-variable, and deep-learning models were evaluated with patient-grouped nested fivefold cross-validation, permutation nulls, and repeated partitions. The same models were then evaluated under image-level fold assignment, and the source of inflation was examined with matching, perturbation, and synthetic-variable controls. Discrimination above chance was not demonstrated: patient-level AUCs were 0.490-0.563, every 95% confidence interval included 0.5, and no upper limit reached 0.70. Changing only fold assignment increased the radiomics-plus-clinical AUC from 0.506 to 0.788 (ΔAUC 0.282; patient-clustered 95% CI 0.209-0.351), and averaging predictions per patient did not remove the inflation (0.504 versus 0.800). Across 20 partitions, mean inflation was 0.363 for age plus lesion size, 0.226 for radiomics, and 0.109 for a B-mode network trained to fit its training data. Random variables held constant within each patient produced similar inflation (0.415), whereas variables varying across images produced none. In a cohort without demonstrable discrimination under patient-grouped validation, image-level fold assignment generated substantial apparent performance. Patient-constant variables acted as identifiers, and patient-level aggregation did not correct the leakage.

articles.title: A Fixed Budget Value Analysis of Few-Shot Medical Vision-Language Model Adaptation.
articles.abstract: Selecting between visual-only and language-informed adaptation is a moving target imaging informatics decision. The same scarce target labels train both the candidate strategies and provide evidence for choosing between them. We introduce a fixed budget, policy value framework for evaluating whether this choice is worthwhile. Four medical vision-language models (BiomedCLIP, PubMedCLIP, MedCLIP, and MedSigLIP) were evaluated across chest radiography and seven MedMNIST tasks at 1-16 shots per class, with external multilabel validation on NIH ChestX-ray14. We compared visual and language-anchored probes and evaluated label-free, support-informed, cross-validated, and held-out meta-selection rules. Policy value was defined as the macro-AUROC gain over always using the visual probe at the same annotation cost. At one shot, language anchoring was superior in 31% of encoder-task combinations, yielding an optimistic oracle opportunity of at most 0.026 macro-AUROC. No deployable selector demonstrated a practically meaningful positive held-out value. Selector value was non-positive at one shot and at most + 0.002 at four shots, with aggregate hierarchical confidence intervals including zero, with the external test demonstrating the same pattern. Harmful language choices were more frequent and larger than beneficial choices, so selection accuracy did not translate into policy value. Controlled class description interventions changed the sign and magnitude of the language effect, demonstrating a genuine yet encoder- and task-dependent opportunity. Under the evaluated fixed budgets, direct visual adaptation was the most dependable use of target labels. Imaging informatics evaluations should report policy value, negative transfer severity, and annotation cost, rather than only selection accuracy.

articles.title: Agreement of CT-Based Renal Volumetry Using Automatic and Semiautomatic Segmentation Tools.
articles.abstract: Renal volume is an important parameter in the follow-up of chronic kidney diseases and surgical planning. Today, software providing three-dimensional (3D) segmentation is widely used in clinical practice. This study aimed to compare the semiautomatic and automatic segmentation methods of 3D Slicer and ITK-SNAP software in terms of renal volume measurements and to evaluate the agreement between these methods. In this retrospective study, abdominal computed tomography (CT) images from 102 individuals were analyzed. Right renal volumes were measured using semiautomatic segmentation with ITK-SNAP and 3D Slicer, and automatic segmentation with TotalSegmentator. Semiautomatic segmentations were performed twice by each of two observers at different times. For Observer 1, a statistically significant difference was observed between the methods in all pairwise comparisons except for the comparison between TotalSegmentator and semiautomatic 3D Slicer segmentation. For Observer 2, statistically significant differences were observed in all pairwise comparisons. Intraobserver and interobserver agreements were high. Regarding segmentation time, statistically significant differences were observed in all pairwise comparisons (p < 0.001), with TotalSegmentator showing significantly shorter segmentation times. This indicates that, although the methods yielded statistically different volume estimates, the measurements showed a consistent pattern across individuals. Overall, the evaluated methods provided consistent renal volume measurements across individuals, although some systematic differences were observed. The findings highlight the importance of considering both agreement and measurement efficiency when selecting a renal volumetry method.

articles.title: Late intra-hepatic arterial complications after severe blunt liver trauma in children: a single-center retrospective cohort.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-operative management is standard for hemodynamically stable pediatric blunt liver trauma, but the incidence and optimal surveillance for late intra-hepatic arterial complications remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To analyze late intra-hepatic arterial complications and their management in a cohort of children with severe blunt liver injury, to confirm a clinical protocol. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients younger than 18 years referred to a quaternary liver center for grade ≥3 blunt liver injury (American Pediatric Surgical Association grading). Demographic and clinical data, imaging findings, active arterial bleeding or pseudoaneurysm not suspected at presentation and/or not detected on initial computerized tomography, and surgical and interventional radiology procedures were collected. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients (median age 14.9 years) with grade III (n=10), IV (n=5), and V (n=17) liver injuries were included. A total of 37 procedures were performed in 19 patients (59%), including peri-hepatic packing, early and delayed surgical explorations, angiography, and 12 embolizations in 11 patients. Overall survival was 100%. In 5 patients (16% of the cohort; all grade IV-V injuries), late intra-hepatic arterial complications were documented on elective follow-up computerized tomography at a median of 10 days after trauma (when patients were asymptomatic), and all were managed successfully by selective interventional radiology, without procedure-related complications. No deaths occurred in this series. CONCLUSIONS: Late intra-hepatic arterial complications were not rare in children with grade IV-V liver injuries. These findings support considering computerized tomography in children with very severe hepatic trauma, around days 10-15 after trauma, to allow pre-emptive interventional radiology management.

articles.title: Diagnostic performance of dual-phase photon-counting detector for localization of parathyroid adenomas after inconclusive first-line imaging.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate diagnostic performance, radiation dose, and quantitative spectral characteristics of dual-phase photon-counting CT (PCD-CT) for parathyroid adenoma localization after inconclusive first-line imaging. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Consecutive patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and negative, discordant, or inconclusive first-line imaging underwent paired [18F]FECh PET/CT and dual-phase PCD-CT with arterial and venous acquisitions. Three radiologists, blinded to clinical and reference-standard information, retrospectively assessed arterial and portal-venous 40- and 70-keV images and VNC reconstructions. The reference standard comprised surgery/histopathology with biochemical confirmation, concordant PET/CT with persistent biochemical disease in nonsurgical positive patients, or clinical/biochemical resolution in negative patients. Lesion-level sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and interreader intraclass correlation (ICC) were calculated. Aorta-normalized attenuation and wash-in and wash-out metrics were compared among adenomas, thyroid tissue, and lymph nodes. RESULTS: Forty-nine patients (mean age, 64.2 ± 10.9 years; 42 women) were included, with 45 patients having 49 reference-standard-positive lesions. PCD-CT lesion-level sensitivity was 67.3%-83.7%, and PPV 67.3%-90.0%, with an interreader agreement of 0.506. Aorta-adjusted wash-out was greater in adenomas (27.2%) than in thyroid (20.2%) and lymph nodes (-3.1%; both p < 0.001). Arterial adenoma-thyroid attenuation and wash-in overlapped between adenomas did not differ significantly (arterial p = 0.615 and thyroid tissue. 0.945 at 40 and 70 keV; wash-in p = 0.363). Mean estimated effective dose was 1.23 ± 0.47 mSv. CONCLUSION: Dual-phase PCD-CT provided reader-dependent parathyroid localization at low radiation dose in a difficult second-line cohort. Quantitative wash-out may aid differentiation from thyroid and lymph-node mimics but requires prospective threshold validation. KEY POINTS: Question Inconclusive first-line imaging complicates parathyroid lesion localization. Findings Reader sensitivity ranged from 67.3% to 83.7% at 1.23 mSv. Critical relevance statement Aorta-adjusted wash-out differed among parathyroid lesions, thyroid tissue, and lymph nodes.

articles.title: Multimodal imaging features of intra-parenchymal schwannoma.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To analyze the CT and MRI features of patients with intra-parenchymal schwannoma. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on the relatively comprehensive conventional and functional CT and/or MRI features of DWI/ADC, MRS, and perfusion from 22 cases of intra-parenchymal schwannoma. RESULTS: There were thirteen men and nine women (median age, 40 years) in this study. The median tumor size was 4.0 cm. Most of the masses located supratentorial. All tumors were well-circumscribed, cystic and solid in 17 cases, solid in four cases and cystic in one case. Hemorrhage in the mass could be observed in two cases, nodular calcification was observed in four cases, and peritumoral edema could be observed in the majority of the cases (n = 15). Most of these lesions presented low-density on plain CT (n = 13/16), iso-hypointense on T1WI and iso-hyperintense on T2WI (n = 20). The solid part of the lesion shows unrestricted diffusion in most of the cases (n = 10/11). After contrast administration, all masses (n = 22) illustrated heterogeneously moderate to marked enhancement and high perfusion with an elevated ratio of maximum relative cerebral blood volume with a value of 10.5 (n = 1). Six cases underwent MRS examination, choline (Cho) peak was slightly elevated, while N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak was not shown or significantly decreased. The Cho/NAA ratio ranged from 0.5 to 2.1. CONCLUSION: A well-defined solid and cystic mass accompanied by prominent vasogenic edema, marked heterogeneous enhancement, low-density on plan CT, unrestricted diffusion, and elevated perfusion within the enhancing solid component, which demonstrates a markedly reduced or nearly absent NAA peak and mildly elevated Cho and MI peaks on MRS, should raise strong clinical suspicion for intra-parenchymal schwannoma.

articles.title: Hippocampal and subfield volume differences in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis: associations with lesion burden and regional MRI involvement.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate global and subfield-specific hippocampal volume differences in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis (POMS) and to examine their associations with white matter lesion burden and MRI-visible hippocampal or temporal lobe involvement. METHODS: The cohort comprised 119 patients with POMS and 120 control participants in a retrospective cross-sectional design. Bilateral hippocampal and subfield volumes were obtained from 3D T1-weighted MRI using the fully automated Hippocampal Subfields Segmentation pipeline and normalized to intracranial volume. White matter lesion burden (total lesion volume, lesion count, and lesion load) was derived using DeepLesionBrain. MRI-visible hippocampal and temporal lobe involvement was assessed by blinded radiologists and related to ipsilateral hippocampal volume using mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Total hippocampal volume normalized to intracranial volume was lower in patients with POMS than in controls (3.14 ± 0.49 vs. 3.41 ± 0.29; 7.8% lower; p < 0.001). Bilateral cornu ammonis subfields (CA1, CA2-CA3, and CA4-DG) and the subiculum showed lower volumes after FDR correction. The most prominent standardized between-group differences involved CA1 and CA4-DG. Higher lesion burden was associated with lower bilateral and overall hippocampal volumes. Ipsilateral hippocampal volume differed significantly across regional involvement categories in both adjusted models (p < 0.001 for each). Direct hippocampal involvement was associated with lower ipsilateral volume than both no involvement and temporal-only involvement, whereas temporal-only involvement did not differ from no involvement. CONCLUSION: POMS is associated with lower global and subfield-specific hippocampal volumes, with a non-uniform pattern across subregions. Hippocampal volume differences were related to both overall lesion burden and direct MRI-visible hippocampal involvement.

articles.title: Intelligent Prediction of WHO/ISUP Grade in Clear-Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Using CT-Based Fusion Delta Features: A Multicenter Study with Biological Interpretability Exploration.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Our study aimed to develop a delta deep learning radiomics model for predicting World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grade in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and to find relevant biomarkers and explore the potential biological mechanisms. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This multicenter cohort of 754 patients with ccRCC from five hospitals was split into training and internal validation cohorts in a 7:3 ratio, along with an external validation cohort (n=221) from three other hospitals. Radiomics and deep learning features were extracted from the tumor regions on multiphase contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT). Delta features were calculated as the absolute differences between features from different imaging phases. The selected features were used to develop delta deep learning radiomics signatures using different classifiers. The diagnostic performance in each model was assessed. Furthermore, gene expression profiling was conducted to for exploratory analysis of biological correlates associated with the model's grade predictions. RESULTS: The delta model achieved AUCs of 0.736 (95% CI 0.671-0.801) and 0.701 (95% CI 0.635-0.768) in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, which were numerically higher than those of the original model based on traditional deep learning radiomics features and demographic baseline clinical model. Additionally, the delta model demonstrated good calibration and a higher net benefit. Bioinformatics and multiomics analysis revealed that high-grade risk-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with inflammation-related pathways, providing preliminary exploratory biological insights into the model's predictions. CONCLUSION: The delta model demonstrated promising performance in WHO/ISUP grade. DEGs in predicted high-grade ccRCC were associated with inflammation-related pathways.

articles.title: Feasibility of prior-informed domain-based electrical impedance tomography for deep tissue thermometry: Phantom experiments and computed tomography-derived numerical simulations.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate monitoring of deep tissue temperature is important during hyperthermia treatment. Because the electrical conductivity of biological tissue generally increases with temperature, Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) may provide a non-invasive approach for estimating temperature changes in deep tissue. PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate a domain-based EIT thermometry framework for quantitative temperature estimation in electrically heterogeneous settings composed of piecewise homogeneous domains, where conventional voxel-based EIT reconstruction is limited by the ill-posed inverse problem and inaccurate separation of domain-level conductivity changes. METHODS: Simulation and phantom studies were performed. In the simulation study, reconstruction performance was evaluated using reconstruction error and stability. In the phantom experiments, performance was evaluated using the mean and maximum absolute temperature errors over reconstructed frames by comparing sensor-measured temperatures with EIT-based estimates. An anatomically realistic model was additionally constructed from a single respiratory phase of one patient computed tomography (CT) dataset, and nine anatomical subdomains were reconstructed under target-centered and external-entry heating scenarios. RESULTS: In the simulation study, the proposed domain-based reconstruction yielded the lowest reconstruction error across the evaluated noise conditions. In phantom experiments, it showed close agreement with direct measurements under all tested conditions. The average conductivity reconstruction error in the homogeneous phantom was 0.29%, while the mean absolute temperature errors in the multi-domain phantoms ranged from 0.22°C to 0.71°C. In pooled phantom comparisons, the proposed method showed mean and maximum absolute temperature errors of 0.44 ± 0.31°C and 0.91 ± 0.77°C, respectively. In the CT-derived model, the mean absolute temperature errors were 0.50°C and 1.43°C for the target-centered and external-entry scenarios, compared with 1.21-1.25°C and 2.60-2.67°C for the benchmark methods, respectively, and the location of the hottest region was preserved in both scenarios. CONCLUSION: The proposed domain-based EIT thermometry demonstrated feasibility in phantom experiments and a CT-derived anatomical model, establishing a foundation for its potential application as a non-invasive temperature monitoring approach.

articles.title: Association between HER2 expression levels and sonographic features in triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between HER2 expression levels and sonographic characteristics in patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 173 patients with pathologically confirmed TNBC. Based on HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) results, patients were classified into three groups: HER2-negative (IHC 0), HER2-low (IHC 1+), and HER2-low (IHC 2 + without amplification as determined by fluorescence in situ hybridization [FISH]). Sonographic features-including tumor shape, orientation, internal echogenicity, margin, posterior acoustic features, and presence of calcification-as well as lymph node metastasis status were compared across the groups. RESULTS: With increasing HER2 expression levels, tumors were more likely to exhibit an irregular shape (p < 0.001), non-circumscribed margins (p = 0.009), reduced incidence of posterior acoustic enhancement (p = 0.004), and higher frequency of calcification (p = 0.026). No significant differences were observed in tumor orientation or internal echogenicity among the groups (p > 0.05). The rate of lymph node metastasis did not differ significantly across the three groups (p = 0.233). CONCLUSION: HER2 expression level is associated with specific sonographic features in TNBC, with higher expression correlating with more suspicious ultrasound characteristics. Although a trend toward increased lymph node metastasis was noted in the HER2-low (IHC 2+) group, this difference was not statistically significant, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: Evaluation of lesion and neoadjuvant treatment response using low-keV dual-energy CT in breast cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exploring the capacity of detecting breast cancer lesion on different monoenergetic images (MEIs) and predicting NAT response using quantitative parameters derived from DECT. METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients with invasive breast cancer who received NAT followed by surgery. Meanwhile, all participants underwent chest DECT and breast MRI before and after NAT. The first end was to assess different MEIs for detecting breast lesion using objective and subjective measurements. The second end was to establish model for predicting pCR using quantitative parameters, and compare the model with visual MRI-rCR. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to analyze prognosis. RESULTS: 199 women with breast cancer were included (median age, 50 years). 52 (26.13%) achieved pCR and 147 (73.87%) were non-pCR after NAT. Low keV MEI had optimal performance to characterize lesion, especially on 40 keV MEI at venous phase (CNR: 6.55, SNR: 7.23, Likert score: 5; all p < 0.001). The multivariable regression showed HER2 positivity (OR, 0.155; 95% CI: 0.061-0.393; p < 0.001) and CT value on 40 keV MEI at venous phase (OR, 1.067; 95% CI: 1.020-1.117; p = 0.005) were independently associated with pCR. The established combined model yielded an AUC of 0.900 (95% CI: 0.856-0.944) when assessed on the full study cohort, beyond the MRI-rCR (AUC, 0.900 vs. 0.782; p = 0.003). The model also showed a nominally significant association with disease-free survival (DFS) on the whole dataset (log-rank, p = 0.046). CONCLUSIONS: MEI with low keV significantly improved visualization of breast cancer. Quantitative parameters derived from 40 keV MEI demonstrated superior value for assessing NAT response and prognosis compared to MRI-rCR. QUESTION: Dual-energy CT has been used for diagnosis of breast lesion. However, the predictive performance to evaluate neoadjuvant treatment response remains unexplored in breast cancer. FINDINGS: Monoenergetic images (MEIs) with low keV has optimal performance for visualization of breast cancer and its quantitative parameters can identify NAT response and prognosis. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Low keV MEI effectively visualizes breast cancer as a complementary examination. Its quantitative parameters at 40 keV MEI demonstrated superior value for assessing NAT response and prognosis compared to MRI-rCR so as to assist clinical strategies. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

articles.title: Fast Voxelwise SNR Estimation for Iterative MRI Reconstructions.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a fast, general-purpose framework for voxelwise noise characterization in iterative MRI reconstructions, recovering the image-domain noise variance, the primary quantity from which SNR, g  -factor, and related image-quality metrics are derived. The framework addresses both the intractability of closed-form formulas beyond Cartesian sampling and the long runtime of pseudo multiple replica (PMR). METHODS: A stochastic noise estimator is proposed that operates in the image domain by Probing the Image-space noise COvariance matrix (PICO) with random probe images. Complex random-phase probes attain minimum kurtosis and reduce estimator variance in the tested reconstruction. PICO was validated against analytical benchmarks and PMR references using Cartesian knee data ( R = 2  ), physical brain phantom data ( R = 2 , 3 , 4  ), in vivo non-Cartesian brain data ( R = 2  ), and compressed-sensing knee reconstructions ( R = 2  ). RESULTS: In Cartesian reconstructions, PICO accurately reproduced analytical SENSE g  -factor maps. In non-Cartesian reconstructions, it achieved 1 %  g  -factor NRMSE ≈ 11 . 9 ×  faster than PMR in a phantom and ≈ 2 . 81 ×  faster in vivo, with the efficiency advantage persisting at higher acceleration. For compressed sensing, the Jacobian-based estimator produced noise maps consistent with PMR and computed them 1 . 84 ×  faster at equal sample counts. Agreement worsened at large added-noise amplitudes and moderate TV strengths. CONCLUSION: PICO targets the exact covariance of fixed linear reconstructions and a first-order covariance for nonlinear reconstructions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to PMR. By reusing existing reconstruction primitives, it could help incorporate voxelwise noise maps into reconstruction workflows.

articles.title: Rigid Motion Estimation Using Accelerated Coordinate Descent (REACT) for MR Imaging.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a computationally viable autofocus method for estimating 3D rigid motion in MR imaging. THEORY AND METHODS: The proposed method, REACT, assumes a piecewise-constant motion trajectory and estimates the rigid motion parameters of individual temporal segments by optimizing an image-quality metric. Coordinate descent is adopted to decompose the high-dimensional optimization problem into a series of subproblems, each updating the motion parameters of a single temporal segment. The cost function of each subproblem is assumed to be approximately locally convex under suitable acquisition conditions. Each subproblem is then solved using a derivative-free solver, thereby avoiding an exhaustive grid search. Numerical simulations investigated the local convexity assumption and data acquisition requirements. REACT was evaluated for respiratory motion correction on in vivo free-breathing coronary MR angiography datasets. Coronary artery sharpness was quantified using unbounded image edge profile acutance (u-IEPA). RESULTS: In numerical simulations, the objective surfaces of the subproblems were approximately locally convex when the current motion estimate was sufficiently close to the desired solution, and REACT required the data collected within each temporal segment to be sufficiently distributed across k  -space. In the in vivo study, REACT yielded higher u-IEPA for both the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the right coronary artery than did a conventional translational motion-estimation method using image-based navigators. REACT also yielded higher u-IEPA for the LAD than did a conventional autofocus nonrigid motion correction method. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the feasibility of coordinate descent for autofocus motion correction in MR imaging.

articles.title: Optimal RF Phase Modulation for Improved Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting T2 Encoding and Efficiency.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To improve magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) T2 encoding by combining phase-based T2 encoding with optimal experiment design. METHODS: Six hundred-timepoint MRF sequences with jointly optimized flip angle (FA) and quadratic RF phase increment schedules were generated by minimizing their Cramér-Rao Lower Bound for tissue dependent sets of T1 and T2. Sequences were optimized for 3T and 0.55T brain MRF and 0.55T prostate MRF and compared against FA-only optimized and unoptimized (600- and 1000-timepoint) sequences. Accuracy and precision were first evaluated using Monte-Carlo Bloch simulations in a digital phantom. Additional simulations identified a spiral interleaf ordering which minimized aliasing artifacts under phase modulation. A T1/T2 phantom was then used to validate simulation results. In vivo performance was assessed in nine healthy subjects, where precision was measured using bootstrap Monte-Carlo experiments with 50 pseudo-replicas. RESULTS: Jointly optimized sequences were found to produce T2 maps with significantly greater accuracy and precision than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences in simulation and phantom experiments (p < 0.001). A Step 5 (37.5° between timepoints) spiral interleaf ordering minimized aliasing under phase modulation, while maintaining comparable performance without. In vivo testing in the brain and prostate revealed higher T2 values, reduced T2 coefficients of variation, and lower B1 + sensitivity than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequence variants. CONCLUSION: Simulation, phantom, and in vivo studies demonstrate that optimized RF phase modulation improves MRF T2 encoding compared to unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences, enabling shorter exams and greater T2 precision in the brain and pelvis at 3T and 0.55T.

articles.title: An On-Premise, Open-Weights Vision-Language Pipeline for Burned-In PHI Removal: Detection, Decision, and Image Degradation on MIDI-B.
articles.abstract: Burned-in protected health information (PHI) in DICOM pixel data blocks multi-site imaging research, and better recognition is assumed to be the route to removal. We asked whether detection or the PHI decision limits removal. A layered pixel pipeline built on Florence-2 OCR was evaluated on MIDI-B with the CBIIT validation script. Against the answer key's OCR-independent coordinates, two controlled arms swapped the engine with the decision fixed, then varied the decision over detections. A nine-condition degradation sweep ran to redaction, with Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests. On clean images, a 0.23 B vision-language model and a CNN OCR at library defaults detected 34/35 and 35/35 regions, flagged the same 10/35 with the decision fixed, and removed the same 33/35. Over fixed detections, Microsoft Presidio flagged 12/35 and a generic rule set 10/35, as 25 of 35 regions are unpatterned markers; redacting every detection reached 35/35, so both shipped misses were decision misses. Under degradation, both engines detected the text in every condition; removal differed most at blur radius 4, 32 versus 26 (p = 0.07), where the CNN OCR misread short markers (exact match 17/25 versus 10/25). An earlier-reported collapse to 18/35 came from a confidence floor in our harness. The strict profile scored 33/35 at 86.7% series accuracy, and the retain profile 32/35 at 97.6%. Removal on clean text is limited by the PHI decision, not the detector. Under synthetic degradation, the engines differ in transcribing short strings, not in detecting them, by a margin this sample cannot resolve. Results are benchmark- and engine-specific.

articles.title: On-Premises Open-Weight Large Language Models for Classifying Epilepsy Brain MRI Reports: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Free-text reports limit the use of imaging data for research cohort screening. This study evaluated whether locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs) can classify brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reports in epilepsy without external data transfer, and which forms of domain knowledge improve classification. In this single-center retrospective study, 1210 epilepsy-protocol brain MRI reports were labeled by a board-certified neuroradiologist for abnormality status and primary imaging finding (eight classes). A held-out test set of 206 reports was classified by a biomedical (OpenBioLLM-8B) and a general-purpose (Qwen3.5-9B) LLM on a single 24-GB graphics processing unit, with and without a rule set and example retrieval, and compared with a fine-tuned radiology-specific BERT model, an independent neuroradiology fellow, and a same-base control model. The primary outcome was the macro-averaged F1 score for the primary finding. Without task-specific training, the general-purpose model achieved a finding macro-F1 of 0.63 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.53-0.70), comparable to the fine-tuned BERT model (0.59; difference, - 0.04; 95% CI, - 0.13 to 0.07) and to inter-reader agreement (0.61; κ = 0.59). A rule set stating institutional category definitions improved the biomedical model (difference, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.11-0.33) without significantly reducing performance in any model, whereas biomedical fine-tuning conferred no advantage over the control model and example retrieval did not help. Residual errors concentrated where the readers disagreed. Locally deployed LLMs performed comparably to inter-reader agreement, which may support human-verified cohort screening; in this institution-specific task, explicit category definitions were more useful than biomedical specialization.

articles.title: Computed tomography-guided percutaneous cryoablation for pediatric osteoid osteoma: clinical success and safety.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Percutaneous thermal ablation has replaced surgery as first-line treatment for osteoid osteoma in many centers. Radiofrequency ablation is the most widely reported technique, whereas cryoablation is an alternative thermal ablation technique. Pediatric data on cryoablation for osteoid osteoma remain limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical and technical success of CT-guided percutaneous cryoablation for osteoid osteoma in children and adolescents. Safety and radiation exposure were assessed as secondary procedural outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 18 consecutive patients (10 males; median age 13.5 years, range 6-17) who underwent CT-guided cryoablation between December 2022 and May 2025. Clinical success at 1 month and technical success were the main outcomes. Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR)-classified adverse events, pain evolution, analgesic use, procedure duration, and dose-length product were recorded as secondary outcomes. Pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS). RESULTS: Technical success was achieved in all procedures (18/18). Clinical success was achieved in all patients by the 1-month clinical follow-up. Median time to complete pain relief was 1 day (interquartile range, 1-2 days); 13/18 patients were pain-free within 24 h, all patients were pain-free within 14 days, and all had discontinued analgesics at 1 month. No SIR-classified procedure-related adverse event was observed in this cohort. Median dose-length product was 158 mGy·cm (interquartile range, 100-300). CONCLUSION: CT-guided cryoablation achieved technical success and complete clinical success at 1 month in this pediatric osteoid osteoma cohort, with rapid pain relief, discontinuation of analgesics, and no SIR-classified procedure-related adverse event observed.

articles.title: Hepatic Ectopic Pregnancy: A 70-Year Systematic Review Focusing on Ultrasound Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: Hepatic ectopic pregnancy (HEP) represents a rare form of abdominal ectopic pregnancy. Its nonspecific clinical present9ation poses a diagnostic challenge, and delayed recognition may culminate in catastrophic intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Scattered case reports provide fragmented descriptions of clinical features, sonographic findings, and treatments. This review aims to provide an overview of HEP and the application of ultrasound in diagnosis and follow up of HEP based on 70 years of published literature.

articles.title: Ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction of intussusception: a practical guide with a focus on low-resource settings.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction (UGHR) is a safe, effective, and reproducible technique for the management of pediatric intussusception. However, there remains a lack of standardized, practical guidance on the implementation and performance of UGHR. OBJECTIVE: To present a practical, standardized framework for UGHR, emphasizing safe implementation across diverse clinical settings. METHODS: This practical review outlines a step-by-step approach based on clinical experience and existing literature, including patient selection, pre-procedural preparation, equipment setup, procedural technique, criteria for success and failure, and troubleshooting strategies. CONCLUSION: The proposed framework is applicable across a wide range of healthcare environments and may be particularly advantageous in low-resource settings where access to fluoroscopic resources is limited.

articles.title: Pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL): a practical clinical guide to contrast-free cerebral perfusion imaging in stroke and steno-occlusive disease.
articles.abstract: The past decade has witnessed the emergence of multiple arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based imaging techniques, with growing evidence supporting their utility across diverse neurological diseases. ASL represents a paradigm shift in perfusion imaging as a noninvasive, contrast-free MRI technique that provides both cerebral perfusion quantification and detection of arterial stenosis or occlusion, offering diagnostic capabilities comparable to the established dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) technique while avoiding contrast-related risks. This review article provides a focused clinically oriented overview of Pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) technique in stroke imaging, discusses the fundamental physical principles of arterial spin labeling, examines various acquisition and optimization strategies, and evaluates clinical applications with primary emphasis on acute ischemic stroke and steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disease, the predominant risk factor for recurrent stroke.

articles.title: Predictive Model for Early Identification of Poor Prognosis in Kidney Transplant Recipients Based on Ultrasound Hemodynamic Parameters Combined with Clinical and Laboratory Indicators: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to identify kidney transplant recipients with functioning grafts at the 3-month post-transplant who were at high risk of subsequent adverse graft outcomes. We developed predictive models and nomograms integrating ultrasound hemodynamic, clinical, and laboratory parameters. METHODS: We analyzed 376 kidney transplant recipients enrolled from January 2020 to April 2023. The 2020-2022 cohort was randomly divided into a training set (n = 200) and an internal random holdout set (validation set 1; n = 131). The subsequently enrolled 2023 cohort was retained as the temporal validation set (validation set 2; n = 45). All ultrasound predictors were assessed at the approximately 3-month post-transplant. Risk factors were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and logistic regression. Predictive models were constructed using logistic regression and 5 machine-learning algorithms. Model performance was evaluated in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, and a nomogram was developed for visualization. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the machine-learning models. RESULTS: The final logistic regression model included graft renal segmental artery resistance index (Grsa RI), preoperative albumin, and postoperative day 5 platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (Po5 PLR). Its AUCs were 0.893 in the internal random holdout set (validation set 1) and 0.859 in the temporal validation set (validation set 2). The random forest model, selected on the basis of the highest training-set AUC among the machine-learning models, achieved AUCs of 0.916 and 0.821 in validation sets 1 and 2, respectively. DeLong tests showed no statistically significant difference in AUC between the logistic regression and random forest models in either validation cohort (p = .958 and p = .561, respectively). Preoperative albumin, Po5 PLR, and Grsa RI were independently associated with adverse graft outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The prediction models effectively identified high-risk recipients using pre- and postoperative variables, providing an actionable strategy for early intervention to improve transplant outcomes by targeting modifiable factors.

articles.title: Combined volume transmit/receive and surface receive-only coils for simultaneous brain and spinal cord imaging of squirrel monkey at 9.4 T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: A combined volume transmit/receive (T/R) and surface receive-only coil was developed for simultaneous anatomical brain and cervical spinal cord imaging of squirrel monkeys at 9.4 T, for which dedicated hardware is lacking in small-bore high-field scanners. METHODS: An Alderman-Grant resonator (AGR) served as the volume T/R coil, and a co-positioned saddle-shaped surface receive coil increased sensitivity over the cervical spinal cord. The two coils produced orthogonal magnetic fields, giving intrinsic geometric decoupling. Bench characterization included unloaded and loaded quality factors. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was measured by gradient-echo imaging of two phantoms, an ex vivo specimen, and a live squirrel monkey, and compared across four receive configurations: a reference quadrature birdcage coil, the AGR alone, the surface coil alone, and the two combined. RESULTS: Inter-coil isolation was -19.9 dB or better under all loading conditions. In vivo, the combined configuration increased cord SNR 2.35-fold over the AGR alone and 2.02-fold over the birdcage coil, giving a brain-to-cord ratio of 1.02 against 2.76. The ex vivo specimen gave a comparable gain over the birdcage coil, ranging from 1.97-fold to 2.21-fold, whereas the more heavily loading saline phantoms gave up to 3.57-fold. Brain SNR was 0.67 to 0.82 times the birdcage value, a deficit already present with the AGR alone and therefore not caused by the surface channel. CONCLUSION: The combined two-channel coil enables simultaneous anatomical imaging of the brain and cervical spinal cord at 9.4 T using only two receive channels.
